newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - Belgian jet engine firm sees blue skies ahead.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Belgian jet engine firm sees blue skies ahead.

text.p: As one arm of Belgium's once-proud FN conglomerate prepares for a change of owner, another declares its troubles are almost over.
Aero-engine company Techspace Aero SA, formerly named FN Moteurs, says it expects orders and earnings to take off in the next four years.

Meantime, Colt Manufacturing Co of the United States has offered three billion Belgian francs ($82.4 million) million) for control of arms maker FN Herstal, aiming to create the world's largest small-calibre arms group.
FN Moteurs and FN Herstal were the two main branches of the FN Group founded in 1889 in the industrial basin of Liege, eastern Belgium, initially to cope with a major arms order from the government.
Using refined blacksmith-based skills, a ready supply of steel and iron and engineering know-how, FN expanded into vehicles, aerospace, agricultural equipment -- and even typewriters and golf clubs.
But growing competition and the need for ever-higher productivity dealt heavy blows to the group in the 1970s and 1980s, forcing it to seek partners in order to survive internationally.
Over capacity and a decline in the dollar also took their toll.

For FN Moteurs, set up as a separate unit at the end of 1987, a French partner was found in 1989. French state aero-engine company Snecma SA, now holding 51 percent, was joined by U.S. engine group Pratt & Whitney, a unit of United Technologies Corp, which has a 19 percent stake.
The remaining shares in FN Moteurs, renamed Techspace Aero in 1992, are held by Belgium's southern region of Wallonia.
BRIGHTER FUTURE
After losses in 1991 the company was recapitalised and 530 jobs were cut, reducing the workforce to 1,150.
But now Techspace sees light at the end of the tunnel. It says efforts to trim debt and restructure are paying off and the order book is looking fuller.

Total debt has been slashed from 6.4 billion francs in 1993 to 3.48 billion in 1996. Net profit rose to 53 million francs from 29 million in 1995. Sales advanced to 5.8 billion francs in 1996 from 5.3 billion in 1995.
In the second half of 1996 the company took on new staff after numbers hit a low of 1,106.
From 1997 to 1999 Techspace expects sales to rise to between 7.6 and eight billion francs. It foresees a positive operating result in 1997 after a loss of 186 million francs in 1996.
It retains its links with big names and big projects.
Techspace hopes to take part in the Airbus A3XX project to make Europe's answer to Boeing's super-jumbo jet, and to extend its participation in the A340 and 100-seater Chinese Airbus projects.
It also expects to increase its work for Ariane 5, the new generation of rockets being developed by the European Space Agency. Techspace has been involved in the Ariane programmes since 1972.
Techspace also has a five percent stake in the project to develop and build the CFM engine, designed to enter service to power Boeing 737 jets at the end of 1997.
CFM is an aircraft engine joint venture between Snecma and General Electric.

Other clients include several European public and private airlines, the airforces of Belgium, the Netherlands, Norway, Denmark and the U.S. Techspace makes components for General Electric and McDonnell Douglas machines.
NO PLACE FOR COMPLACENCY
But the company says it cannot be complacent and must continue its drive to boost productivity, warning that a downturn could hit the global aerospace industry at the beginning of the next century.
"We must increase our productivity before the probable next crisis, expected for 2001-2002," spokesman Ferdinand Lippens told Reuters.
"Our financial structure is better but still fragile," he added.
Competition is fierce and Techspace sees itself as a small fish in a big pond. Its names its main competitors as AB Volvo, Fiat Avio, ITP of Spain, Dasa, BMW and Germany's MTU.
The ever-present threat of currency turmoil also hangs over Techspace, a small exporter in a heavily dollar-sensitive industry.

To deal with the challenges it plans to invest heavily in research and development -- spending 2.5 billion francs in the next four years -- to maintain its edge as a maker of high-tech components and an engine servicing company.
($ = 36.39 Belgian Francs)
